x: In 1913, Indian revolutionaries living in the United States of America and Canada formed the Ghadar (Rebellion) Party. The majority of the party's members were Punjabi Sikh peasants and ex-soldiers who had come to North America in search of employment but experienced severe discrimination based on their race and economic status. The Association established a headquarters, Yugantar Ashram, in San Francisco and started a weekly paper, the Ghadar, for free circulation. • Aim: The Ghadar Party pledged to wage a revolutionary war against the British in India. • Ideology: Though most of the party's members were Punjabi Sikh peasants and ex-soldiers, the party's ideology was strongly secular. In the words of Sohan Singh Bhakna, who later became a major peasant leader of Punjab: "We were not Sikhs or Punjabis. Our religion was patriotism". • Presence: In addition to North America, particularly Canada and the United States of America, the party had active members in other countries such as Mexico, Japan, China, the Philippines, Malaya, Singapore, Thailand, Indo-China, and East and South Africa. Modern Indian History PMF IAS IH – 98 • Leaders: Lala Har Dayal, Mohammed Barkatullah, Bhagwan Singh, Ram Chandra and Sohan Singh Bhakna were some of the prominent leaders of the Ghadar Party.

x: The Kamagatamaru was a Japanese steamliner chartered by an affluent Punjabi businessman, Gurdit Singh to bring Indian immigrants to Canada. The ship departed in 1914 A.D., taking 376 Indians for Canada’s Vancouver port, but the Canadian police refused their entry in Canada. A Shore Committee was constituted to protect the rights of Indian travellers under the leadership of Hussain Rahim, Balwant Singh, and Sohan Lal Pathak. Annie Besant was a prominent Theosophist, educationist, social reformer and nationalist leader. She played a vital role in India's freedom movement through her writings, speeches and the Home Rule Movement. To spread nationalist ideas and mobilize public opinion, she founded two influential newspapers:
• New India – A daily newspaper that strongly advocated self-government, constitutional reforms and Indian nationalism.
• Common Weal – A weekly journal that discussed political, educational and social issues while supporting the Home Rule Movement. Through these newspapers, Annie Besant criticized British policies and inspired educated Indians to participate actively in the national movement. She also founded the Home Rule League in 1916 and became the first woman President of the Indian National Congress in 1917. Hence, the correct answer is Option (3).

s:
